questions.statement: Choose the pattern that correctly forms the zero conditional.
questions.context: A teacher reviews the three basic conditional patterns with the class before the unit test.

options.text: If + present simple, present simple
options.feedback: The zero conditional uses the present simple in both clauses because the result is always true.

options.text: If + present simple, will + infinitive
options.feedback: If plus present simple with will is the first conditional, which describes a real future possibility.

options.text: If + past simple, would + infinitive
options.feedback: If plus past simple with would is the second conditional, which describes an unreal situation.

options.text: If + past perfect, would have + participle
options.feedback: If plus past perfect with would have is the third conditional, which refers to an unreal past.

questions.explanation:
The zero conditional keeps the present simple in both the if clause and the result clause. It states facts that are always true.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the pattern that correctly forms the first conditional.
questions.context: A student is making flashcards to memorise the conditionals before the Friday quiz.

options.text: If + present simple, present simple
options.feedback: Present simple in both clauses forms the zero conditional, which is used for general truths instead.

options.text: If + present simple, will + infinitive
options.feedback: The first conditional takes the present simple after if and will plus the infinitive in the result clause.

options.text: If + past simple, would + infinitive
options.feedback: Past simple with would forms the second conditional, which talks about imaginary situations.

options.text: If + present simple, would + infinitive
options.feedback: Would cannot follow a present simple if clause, because that mixture does not belong to any pattern.

questions.explanation:
The first conditional links a real future condition in the present simple with a result in will plus the infinitive.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the pattern that correctly forms the second conditional.
questions.context: A tutor explains the pattern that English uses for dreams and imaginary situations.

options.text: If + present simple, will + infinitive
options.feedback: Present simple with will is the first conditional, which describes real future chances.

options.text: If + past simple, will + infinitive
options.feedback: Past simple with will mixes two different patterns, and the imagined result needs would.

options.text: If + past simple, would + infinitive
options.feedback: The second conditional uses the past simple after if and would plus the infinitive for the imagined result.

options.text: If + present perfect, would + infinitive
options.feedback: The present perfect is not part of this pattern, because the if clause needs the past simple.

questions.explanation:
Unreal situations take the second conditional: past simple in the if clause and would plus the infinitive in the result.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Explain why the sentence If you heat ice, it melts uses two present simple verbs.
questions.context: A student asks the teacher why the sentence has no will anywhere in it.

options.text: Because the zero conditional describes one single event tomorrow
options.feedback: A single future event would need the first conditional, which puts will in the result clause.

options.text: Because the zero conditional imagines a situation that is impossible
options.feedback: An impossible situation belongs to the second conditional, which uses the past simple and would.

options.text: Because the zero conditional reports an event that finished yesterday
options.feedback: A finished event would need past tenses, as the third conditional does for unreal pasts.

options.text: Because the zero conditional states facts that are always true
options.feedback: The zero conditional expresses general truths, so the present simple appears in both clauses.

questions.explanation:
Melting ice is a scientific rule, and scientific rules take the zero conditional with the present simple in both clauses.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Read the sentence and choose what it expresses: If the bus arrives late, we will miss the museum.
questions.context: Marta tells her classmate about her plans for the school trip next week.

options.text: A real possibility in the future and its likely result
options.feedback: Present simple with will is the first conditional, used for future situations the speaker sees as possible.

options.text: A general truth that never changes
options.feedback: A general truth needs the zero conditional, with the present simple in both clauses and no will.

options.text: An imaginary situation that will never happen
options.feedback: An imaginary situation is expressed by the second conditional, which uses would instead of will.

options.text: A regret about something that did not happen
options.feedback: A regret about the past would use the third conditional, which needs had plus a participle.

questions.explanation:
This sentence is a first conditional: the speaker considers the late bus possible, so the result clause takes will.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Read the sentence and choose what it suggests: If I had a yacht, I would sail to Ibiza.
questions.context: Diego is describing a daydream during the break at his school in Valencia.

options.text: The situation is a fixed fact about the sea near Ibiza
options.feedback: A fixed fact would be a zero conditional sentence, with the present simple in both parts.

options.text: The situation is imaginary, because Diego does not have a yacht
options.feedback: Past simple with would is the second conditional, which signals that the situation is unreal or imagined.

options.text: The situation is a firm plan for next summer
options.feedback: A firm plan for the future fits the first conditional, which uses will for the result.

options.text: The situation is a promise about an exam next week
options.feedback: A promise about the future also takes the first conditional, because the speaker sees it as possible.

questions.explanation:
Because Diego uses had and would, he signals distance from reality: he is imagining a yacht, not planning one.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Complete the zero conditional: If you heat water to 100 degrees, it ___.
questions.context: A science teacher in Madrid writes a rule about water on the whiteboard.

options.text: will boil
options.feedback: Will boil belongs to the first conditional, but a scientific fact does not describe one future event.

options.text: would boil
options.feedback: Would boil would turn the sentence into a second conditional and suggest the boiling is imaginary.

options.text: boils
options.feedback: The zero conditional needs the present simple in the result clause, so boils is correct.

options.text: boiled
options.feedback: Boiled is past simple, but the zero conditional describes what is always true, so the past is wrong.

questions.explanation:
Water boiling at 100 degrees is a general law, and general laws take the present simple in both clauses of a zero conditional.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Complete the first conditional: If it rains tomorrow, we ___ the match.
questions.context: Lucia checks the weather forecast before the football match on Saturday.

options.text: cancel
options.feedback: Cancel alone would make this a zero conditional, but one specific Saturday is not a general truth.

options.text: would cancel
options.feedback: Would cancel creates the second conditional, which would present the rain as imaginary.

options.text: will cancelled
options.feedback: Will must be followed by the bare infinitive, so will cancelled is not a possible form.

options.text: will cancel
options.feedback: The first conditional puts will plus the bare infinitive in the result clause, so will cancel fits.

questions.explanation:
A real future possibility takes the first conditional: present simple after if and will plus infinitive in the result.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Complete the second conditional: If I ___ rich, I would buy my parents a house.
questions.context: A student imagines a different life while writing a class essay about dreams.

options.text: were
options.feedback: The second conditional needs the past simple after if, and were is the classic form for this meaning.

options.text: am
options.feedback: Am is present simple, which belongs to the zero or first conditional, not to an imaginary one.

options.text: will be
options.feedback: Will be is a future form, and the if clause of a second conditional never takes will.

options.text: would be
options.feedback: Would be cannot appear in the if clause, because would belongs only in the result clause.

questions.explanation:
For the imagined state of being rich, the if clause takes the past simple, and were is the standard second conditional form.

questions.statement: Classify this sentence: If she studies hard, she will pass the exam.
questions.context: Two classmates compare sentences from their homework before handing it in.

options.text: Zero conditional
options.feedback: The zero conditional would need the present simple in both clauses, without will.

options.text: First conditional
options.feedback: Present simple after if with will in the result is the exact shape of the first conditional.

options.text: Second conditional
options.feedback: The second conditional would need the past simple after if and would in the result.

options.text: Third conditional
options.feedback: The third conditional would need the past perfect and would have, referring to the past.

questions.explanation:
The verb forms give it away: studies is present simple and will pass carries will, the signature of the first conditional.

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that is a zero conditional.
questions.context: A teacher asks the class to sort example sentences into three groups by type.

options.text: If you mix blue and yellow, you will get green
options.feedback: Will in the result clause makes this a first conditional, treating the mixing as one future event.

options.text: If you mixed blue and yellow, you would get green
options.feedback: Mixed with would is the second conditional, which would imagine the mixing as unreal.

options.text: If you mix blue and yellow, you get green
options.feedback: Present simple in both clauses marks the zero conditional, which fits a permanent colour fact.

options.text: If you had mixed blue and yellow, you would have got green
options.feedback: Had mixed with would have is the third conditional, which imagines a different past.

questions.explanation:
Colour mixing is a permanent rule of paint, so the zero conditional with two present simple verbs is the right choice.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that is a second conditional.
questions.context: The class continues the sorting activity with sentences about imaginary plans.

options.text: If I live by the sea, I will swim every morning
options.feedback: Live with will swim is the first conditional, which treats the move to the coast as possible.

options.text: If I live by the sea, I swim every morning
options.feedback: Live with swim is the zero conditional, which would describe a habit that is always true.

options.text: If I had lived by the sea, I would have swum every morning
options.feedback: Had lived with would have swum is the third conditional, which imagines a different past.

options.text: If I lived by the sea, I would swim every morning
options.feedback: Lived with would swim is the past simple plus would pattern that defines the second conditional.

questions.explanation:
Only the past simple lived with would swim creates the distance from reality that the second conditional needs.

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that gives a real warning about tonight.
questions.context: Pablo wants to warn his younger brother about a realistic risk before the party tonight.

options.text: If you arrive after midnight, Mum will be angry
options.feedback: A real warning about tonight takes the first conditional, because the danger is genuinely possible.

options.text: If you arrive after midnight, Mum is angry
options.feedback: Mum is angry in a zero conditional describes a permanent fact, not a warning about one night.

options.text: If you arrived after midnight, Mum would be angry
options.feedback: Would be in the second conditional suggests the anger is imaginary, which weakens a real warning.

options.text: If you had arrived after midnight, Mum would have been angry
options.feedback: Would have been in the third conditional looks back at a past party that cannot change.

questions.explanation:
Tonight is a real future situation, so the warning uses the first conditional with will in the result clause.

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that gives advice in the softest way.
questions.context: A student wants to give advice in a gentle way during a speaking exam.

options.text: If I am you, I apologise today
options.feedback: The pattern if I am you does not exist in English; the fixed form is if I were you.

options.text: If I were you, I would apologise today
options.feedback: If I were you with would is the fixed second conditional pattern used to soften advice.

options.text: If I am you, I will apologise today
options.feedback: Am you with will mixes a present form with a future result, so no speaker says it.

options.text: If I were you, I apologise today
options.feedback: Were without would breaks the pattern, and the soft advice structure needs would plus the infinitive.

questions.explanation:
If I were you plus would is the classic way to soften advice, because it places the advice in an imagined world.

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that is written correctly.
questions.context: A teacher marks the common mistakes from the homework on the whiteboard.

options.text: If she had more time, she will learn the guitar
options.feedback: Will cannot follow a past simple if clause, because the imagined result needs would.

options.text: If she has more time, she would learn the guitar
options.feedback: Has with would joins the clauses of two different conditionals, so the sentence fails.

options.text: If she had more time, she would learn the guitar
options.feedback: Had with would learn matches the second conditional, which fits an imaginary lack of time.

options.text: If she would have more time, she learns the guitar
options.feedback: Would does not belong in the if clause, and learns in the result describes a habit, not a dream.

questions.explanation:
The imagined lack of time requires the second conditional: past simple had after if and would plus the infinitive.

questions.statement: Choose the sentence about the lottery that is written correctly.
questions.context: The teacher continues with trickier examples where both clauses must match.

options.text: If I will win the lottery, I would travel the world
options.feedback: Will never appears in the if clause of a second conditional, which takes the past simple.

options.text: If I won the lottery, I will travel the world
options.feedback: Won with will mixes a second conditional condition with a first conditional result.

options.text: If I would win the lottery, I travel the world
options.feedback: Would cannot start the if clause, and travel in the result reads as a habit, not a dream.

options.text: If I won the lottery, I would travel the world
options.feedback: Won with would travel is a correct second conditional, imagining an unlikely future win.

questions.explanation:
An unlikely future win takes the second conditional, so the if clause needs won and the result needs would travel.

questions.statement: Compare these two sentences: If we book now, we will pay less. If we booked now, we would pay less. Then choose the difference between them.
questions.context: A student compares two sentences about the same trip to understand the difference.

options.text: The first imagines booking as unlikely and the second sees it as possible
options.feedback: Booked with would is the second conditional, which presents the booking as unlikely or imaginary.

options.text: The first is about the past and the second is about the future
options.feedback: Neither sentence contains a past perfect form, so neither one refers to the past.

options.text: The first is a general truth and the second is a regret
options.feedback: A general truth would take the zero conditional and a regret would take the third.

options.text: Both sentences mean exactly the same thing
options.feedback: The two conditionals signal different likelihood, so the meanings do not match.

questions.explanation:
Would plus the past simple adds distance from reality, so the second sentence treats booking as less likely than the first.

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that expresses a future plan depending on a real condition.
questions.context: Sofia writes a message to her host family in Dublin about her weekend plans.

options.text: If the weather were fine on Sunday, we would go to the coast
options.feedback: Were with would go imagines the weather as unreal, which does not fit a genuine plan.

options.text: If the weather is fine on Sunday, we will go to the coast
options.feedback: Is with will go is the first conditional, which fits a real plan that depends on the forecast.

options.text: If the weather is fine on Sunday, we go to the coast
options.feedback: Go without will reads as a zero conditional habit, which cannot describe one specific Sunday.

options.text: If the weather had been fine on Sunday, we would have gone to the coast
options.feedback: Had been with would have gone refers to a past Sunday, so the plan could no longer change.

questions.explanation:
A plan for this Sunday depends on real weather, so the first conditional with will is the natural choice.

questions.statement: Explain why If I were a bird, I would fly over the mountains is a correct second conditional.
questions.context: During revision the teacher asks students to defend the tenses in model sentences.

options.text: Because were and would show that the speaker describes a routine
options.feedback: A routine would need the zero conditional, with the present simple in both clauses.

options.text: Because were and would show that the speaker remembers a flight
options.feedback: A memory of a real flight would use past forms throughout, without would.

options.text: Because were and would show that the speaker is only imagining
options.feedback: The past simple with would creates the unreal distance that defines the second conditional.

options.text: Because were and would show that the speaker predicts a certain future
options.feedback: A certain prediction about the future takes the first conditional with will, not would.

questions.explanation:
Were plus would signal that the speaker is not really a bird, which is exactly the unreal meaning the second conditional carries.

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that talks about an imaginary situation rather than a real plan.
questions.context: A student finishes a class survey about dreams and real plans at a school in Seville.

options.text: If I speak Japanese, I will work as a translator
options.feedback: Speak with will work treats learning Japanese as a real option, so it is a first conditional plan.

options.text: If I speak Japanese, I work as a translator
options.feedback: Speak with work states a general rule and fits the zero conditional, not an imaginary case.

options.text: If I spoke Japanese, I will work as a translator
options.feedback: Spoke with will mixes a second conditional condition with a first conditional result.

options.text: If I spoke Japanese, I would work as a translator
options.feedback: Spoke with would work presents Japanese as a skill the speaker lacks, an imagined situation.

questions.explanation:
Spoke with would work creates distance from reality, so the sentence clearly imagines a skill the speaker does not have.
